identity.plain_name: A thin, gently sloping block (wedge) pushed or tapped into a gap so it jams tight and stays there by friction, squeezing the parts together until you knock it back out from the thin end
identity.term: Self-locking wedge (friction wedge; as a machine part: taper key or cotter)
aliases: folding wedges (a pair of wedges driven towards each other; 'cramping' with folding wedges in old joinery books) (Wikimedia Commons, Cassell's Carpentry; Engineering Statics)
wedge clamp / wedge clamping (Fine Woodworking; Printables 'CNC Wedge Clamp')
taper key; gib-head key or 'gip head' key (DIN 6887) (Wikipedia 'Key (engineering)'; MBO Osswald)
tangential taper key (pairs of taper keys for heavy torque) (Wikipedia 'Key (engineering)'; Thang 'Wedge mechanism 23')
cotter / cotter pin (British usage; a tapered pin with a flat, e.g. bicycle crank cotter; in the US 'cotter pin' means a split pin instead) (Wikipedia 'Cotter (pin)')
Dutch pin (tapered pin driven into a hole drilled across shaft and hub) (Wikipedia 'Key (engineering)')
wedged tenon, tusk tenon wedge, loose wedge (woodworking) (Popular Woodworking; Woodsmith)
quoin (printing), wheel chock (listed under 'See also' on Wikipedia 'Wedge')
identity.one_liner: A shallow wedge driven into a gap multiplies a light tap into a strong squeeze, and because its slope is gentle, friction stops it sliding back out, so it holds parts tight until it is knocked out again.
identity.complexity: Single piece (the wedge) working against the two parts it jams between; folding wedges are a matched pair; a taper key is one tapered bar in a matching tapered keyway in the hub (Wikipedia 'Key (engineering)'); a bicycle cotter is a tapered pin with a flat face, a threaded end, a washer and a nut (Wikipedia 'Cotter (pin)').
identity.how_it_works: Pushing a wedge along its length moves its sloping face sideways only a little, so a light push or tap becomes a much larger sideways squeeze; the mechanical advantage is roughly its length divided by its thickness (Wikipedia 'Wedge'). The squeeze presses the wedge's faces hard against the parts, and friction on those faces resists it sliding back. If the slope is shallow enough (the wedge angle is smaller than the 'friction angle', arctan of the friction coefficient) friction wins and the wedge stays put after you stop pushing: it is self-locking (Wikipedia 'Wedge'; IIT Guwahati ME101 notes). To release it you drive it back from the thin end, pull it by a head, or push it out with another wedge (a drift) (Wikipedia 'Machine taper'; MBO Osswald).

job: join and hold: jams parts together, e.g. a hub on a shaft with a taper key, a crank on its axle with a cotter, a tenon in a mortise with wedges
lock, and release by hand: a door wedge or a tusk-tenon wedge is kicked or tapped in to hold and tapped out to release
tighten and hold tension: driving a wedge (or a pair of folding wedges) in further squeezes parts together like a clamp and keeps the pressure on (Fine Woodworking; Engineering Statics)

line parts up exactly: shims and adjusting wedges set a gap or level a part, e.g. a wedge that adjusts the gap between a slide and its runway (Thang 'Wedge mechanism 17') and shims under machine feet (Wikipedia 'Shim (spacer)')
finder_attributes.motion: slide: the wedge slides a short way into the gap while it is driven, then nothing moves (none once seated)
finder_attributes.degrees_of_freedom: 0 once driven home: the wedge and the parts it jams are locked by friction. While fitting, the wedge has 1 (sliding along its taper).
special_behaviour: self-locking (holds under load, won't back-drive): a shallow wedge cannot be pushed back out by the force it is holding, because friction on its faces is bigger than the push-back (Engineering Statics: 'high-friction (self-locking) wedges'; Wikipedia 'Wedge')
tensioning (takes up slack and holds): driving it further takes up any gap and adds clamping force, and a loose wedge can be re-tightened with a tap (Woodsmith on tusk tenons)
quick-release: simple wedges come out with a kick or a tap from the thin end, with no fasteners to undo (Wikipedia 'Doorstop'; Woodsmith)
holding_principle: friction or clamping (force-fit): the wedge itself is held only by friction on its sloping faces, and the parts are held by the squeeze it produces; a taper key transmits force by friction on its inclined faces rather than by shape (MBO Osswald)

shape (the parts interlock; form-fit): in a cotter joint, a tusk tenon or a wedged tenon the wedge also blocks the parts from pulling apart, so the joint is locked by shape once the wedge is in (Thang 'Wedge mechanism 21'; Woodsmith; Popular Woodworking)
finder_attributes.input_output: not applicable as a holding joint. As a mechanism, a wedge turns a push along its length into a smaller but stronger sideways movement (mechanical advantage about length / width; Wikipedia 'Wedge'); a self-locking wedge cannot be driven backwards by its load (back-drivable: no), though vibration can walk it out (Sheldon Brown on cotters).
finder_attributes.power: passive (no power needed): it is driven in by hand, a mallet or hammer, and stays by friction
finder_attributes.removability: removable: knocked back out from the thin end, pulled by its head (gib-head key, with a key puller) or pushed out with a drift (Wikipedia 'Machine taper'; MBO Osswald). Glued wedges in wedged through-tenons are effectively permanent (Popular Woodworking).
finder_attributes.reuse_cycles: many times for door wedges, folding wedges and tusk-tenon wedges (Woodsmith: tusk tenons can be taken apart); a few times for tightly driven metal cotters and taper keys, which are often damaged on removal (Sheldon Brown: threads mushroom and cotters may have to be drilled out)
finder_attributes.tools_needed: None for a door wedge; a mallet or hammer to drive and release most wedges; a drift or punch to drive out a tight one; a key puller for gib-head keys (MBO Osswald); a cotter press or hammer, punch and locking pliers for bicycle cotters (Sheldon Brown). To make wooden wedges: a bandsaw (or saw) and optionally a plane (Fine Woodworking).
finder_attributes.load: Medium to heavy in the direction it squeezes (a small tap produces a large clamping force; high-friction wedges hold shoring timbers in ships' damage control, per Engineering Statics). Taper keys transmit shaft torque and resist vibration and shock loads (MBO Osswald). Weak against vibration and repeated load reversals, which can loosen it (Sheldon Brown), against being pushed from the thin end, and in wood against splitting of the part it presses on (Woodsmith; Popular Woodworking).
finder_attributes.adjustable: yes: drive it further to tighten or to take up wear or wood shrinkage; e.g. a tusk-tenon wedge can be re-tightened with a tap when seasonal wood movement loosens the joint (Woodsmith); wedges can set a gap between a slide and its runway (Thang 'Wedge mechanism 17')
finder_attributes.play_and_precision: No play once driven: taper keys 'eliminate potential play' compared with plain parallel keys (MBO Osswald). But a taper key can push the hub slightly off-centre on the shaft (Wikipedia 'Key (engineering)'), and the final position depends on how hard it is driven; the angle of a bicycle cotter's flat decides where the crank ends up, so mismatched cotters leave the cranks out of line (Wikipedia 'Cotter (pin)'; Sheldon Brown). Wedges are very tolerant of rough, uneven gaps, which is why shims and wedges are used for levelling (Wikipedia 'Shim (spacer)').
finder_attributes.access_needed: both sides: a through wedge, cotter or tusk tenon is driven in from the thick end and knocked out from the thin end. A door wedge or shim needs only one side, and a gib-head taper key is fitted and pulled from the end of the shaft.
finder_attributes.materials: Straight-grained hardwood for joinery wedges, often a contrasting colour (Popular Woodworking); saw-cut surfaces grip better for clamping wedges, smooth surfaces are easier to remove, and oily woods such as teak or lignum vitae make self-lubricating removable wedges (Fine Woodworking 1992); wood, rubber, fabric or plastic door wedges (Wikipedia 'Doorstop'); steel or stainless steel taper keys (MBO Osswald); steel cotters; wood, plastic, metal or even paper shims (Wikipedia 'Shim (spacer)'); TPU for grippy printed door wedges (Printables model 1612035).
finder_attributes.maker_difficulty: easy: a wedge is quick to cut on a bandsaw or print in one piece; matching its angle to a tapered slot (tusk tenon, taper key) takes more care, so moderate for those

processes: woodwork: sawn or bandsawn wedges, wedged and tusk tenons, folding wedges for clamping
3D print (FDM): door wedges, wedge clamps and printed wedge-locked joints (Printables models)
CNC: milled wedge clamps and tapered keyways; laser-cut 'hammer joints' with a wedge through a tenon (Printables 'Tenon Wedge Hammer Joint Test' was adapted from a laser-cut design)
laser cut: flat wedges and wedged tab joints in sheet material [uncertain: no specific design guide found]
off-the-shelf part: taper keys (DIN 6887), tapered shims, rubber door wedges, bicycle cotters
making.print_in_place: no: the wedge is printed separately and driven in after the other parts are assembled
making.making_tips_3d_printing: 1) Keep the slope shallow so it self-locks: the wedge angle must be smaller than the friction angle (arctan of the friction coefficient) (Wikipedia 'Wedge'); for a clamping wedge about 1 in 6 (roughly 9.5 degrees) is a good starting point (Fine Woodworking 1992), and joinery wedges use about 3 to 5 degrees (Popular Woodworking; Woodsmith). 2) Print the wedge lying flat on its broad face so the sloping faces are smooth top and bottom surfaces rather than stair-stepped [uncertain: reasoning, not a tested rule]. 3) Test designs are printed in PLA with 2 perimeters and 15% gyroid infill and tapped home with a soft hammer (Printables 'Tenon Wedge Hammer Joint Test' by kaje); a strong filament such as carbon-fibre polycarbonate is used for CNC wedge clamps (Printables 'CNC Pivoting Wedge Clamp' by Elphwrkz). 4) Use TPU (about 90A to 95A) for door wedges that must grip the floor; PLA or PETG grip less (Printables 'Flexible TPU Door Stopper'). 5) Expect it to loosen over time: printed PLA parts creep under constant load (PMC7764475 creep study), and PLA softens above about 60 C (Prusa), so a wedge left under constant pressure, or in a hot place, will relax; check and re-tap it, or use PETG or a harder material. 6) Leave plenty of material beyond the slot the wedge presses on, because it pushes hard on the end: woodworkers leave at least 1/2 in of wood beyond a tusk-tenon wedge mortise (Woodsmith) [uncertain: the equivalent for printed parts is not tested]. 7) Add small teeth or texture for more grip in soft materials such as cloth (Printables 'Wedge Tensioner / Clamp for Canvas' uses 'strong teeth').
making.off_the_shelf_parts: Search for: 'taper key' or 'gib head key DIN 6887' (1:100 taper; e.g. MBO Osswald (brand)); 'taper pin'; 'bicycle cotter pin' (cottered cranks); 'tapered shims' or 'shim stock' and 'laminated shims'; 'door wedge' or 'door stop wedge' (rubber); 'folding wedges' or 'timber wedges' (construction); 'plug and feathers' (stone splitting wedges); 'felling wedge'; 'drift' (for knocking out Morse-taper tools); 'key puller'.
rules_of_thumb: Self-locking condition: a wedge binds (stays put) when its angle is less than the arctangent of the friction coefficient (Wikipedia 'Wedge'). Statics texts show that with friction on both faces a wedge stays in place up to about twice the friction angle (IIT Guwahati ME101 lecture 14), so keeping the angle below arctan(mu) is the safe rule. Example: mu = 0.3 gives arctan(0.3) = about 17 degrees (calculated).

For clamping with wedges, 'a wedge that rises about 1 in. in 6 in. makes a good choice'; steep wedges give more movement but need more force and are more likely to slip (Blandford, 'Clamping with Wedges', Fine Woodworking #93).

Wedged through-tenons: a 3-degree taper on the mortise ends and wedges works well, with the taper extending about three-quarters of the way down the mortise (Popular Woodworking, 'Wedged Mortise and Tenon').

Tusk tenons: wedge and wedge mortise with a matching bevel of about 5 degrees; a loose-wedge (dovetailed) version uses about 10 to 12 degrees; leave at least 1/2 in of solid wood beyond the wedge mortise to avoid splitting (Woodsmith).
Taper keys (gib-head, DIN 6887) have a 1:100 taper, are driven in with a hammer and hold by friction; sizes run from 4 x 4 x 14 to 50 x 28 x 400 mm for shafts of 10 to 230 mm (MBO Osswald).
Morse tapers (a self-holding taper, which is a wedge wrapped round a cone) are about 1.49 degrees (roughly 3 degrees included), about 1:20 (Wikipedia 'Machine taper').

Cotters: hammer in, snug the nut, hammer again and repeat until no more slack appears; don't try to pull them in with the nut alone (it strips the thread); re-tap and re-tighten after about 50 miles of riding (Sheldon Brown, 'Cottered Cranks').

everyday_examples: A door wedge kicked under a door to hold it open (Wikipedia 'Doorstop')
A folded card or shim under a wobbly table leg (Wikipedia 'Shim (spacer)')
The wooden wedge that holds the blade in a traditional hand plane (Fine Woodworking, 'The Versatile Wedge')
Cottered cranks on older bicycles, and the wedge inside a bicycle quill stem (Wikipedia 'Cotter (pin)'; Wikipedia 'Wedge'; Thang 'Wedge mechanism 19')
guidance.when_to_use: Use a wedge when you want a strong, tight hold that is quick to make and can be undone with a tap: knock-down furniture joints (tusk tenons), locking a tenon permanently (glued wedged tenons), clamping awkward or thin glue-ups where ordinary clamps don't fit (Fine Woodworking), taking up an uneven or unknown gap (shims, levelling), holding a door or a part in place temporarily, fixing a hub to a shaft without play in heavy, vibrating machinery (taper keys; MBO Osswald), and gently prising parts apart without damage (Fine Woodworking).
guidance.when_not_to_use: Avoid it where there is strong vibration or load reversal and nobody will check it, because wedges and cotters can work loose (Sheldon Brown); use a screw with a lock nut or threadlocker, or a pin that can't slide. Avoid it where the hub must run exactly centred, because a taper key can push the hub off-centre (Wikipedia 'Key (engineering)'); use a parallel key, a keyless locking bush or a taper-lock bush. Avoid steep wedges in slippery materials (they pop out; Fine Woodworking 1992) and wedging close to the end of wood or thin printed walls (they split; Woodsmith). For something you undo often, a cam lever, toggle clamp or quick-release pin is faster and needs no hammer.
guidance.environment_limits: Wood shrinks and swells with humidity, so wooden wedges loosen as wood dries and may need re-tapping (Woodsmith); swelling can also make wedges grip harder, as ancient quarrymen used wet wooden wedges to split stone (Wikipedia 'Wedge'). Vibration can walk wedges and cotters loose (Sheldon Brown); a tusk-tenon wedge oriented vertically is less likely to work loose (Woodsmith). Printed plastic wedges creep under constant load (PMC7764475 creep study) and PLA softens above about 60 C (Prusa), so the clamping force fades over time and in heat. Oil or grease on the faces reduces friction and can let a wedge slip out [uncertain: general principle, no specific source].
guidance.safety_notes: Hammering: miss-hits damage parts and hands; hold a punch or drift with locking pliers, not your fingers (Sheldon Brown). Hammered steel ends mushroom and can chip [uncertain]. Heating a part to free a stuck cotter weakens it (Sheldon Brown). A wedge holding up a load (shoring, levelling a machine) can release suddenly if knocked or if it slips, dropping the load, so keep clear and block the load before removing it [uncertain: general practice]. Driving wedges near the end of wood can split it suddenly (Woodsmith).
guidance.common_failures: 1) Works loose from vibration, wood shrinkage or plastic creep: re-tap it, orient it so gravity and vibration don't push it out (Woodsmith), or add a nut or pin (Sheldon Brown: re-tighten cotters after about 50 miles). 2) Too steep, so it slips out: make the slope shallower or roughen the faces (Fine Woodworking 1992). 3) Splits the part it presses on: leave more material beyond the slot, drill relief holes at the end of saw kerfs in wedged tenons (Popular Woodworking), and match the wedge angle to the slot so pressure is spread (Woodsmith). 4) Taper key pushes the hub off-centre (Wikipedia 'Key (engineering)'). 5) Mismatched cotters leave cranks out of line (Wikipedia 'Cotter (pin)'). 6) Stuck fast: needs sharp, well-aimed hammer blows, a punch, drilling out or (last resort) heat (Sheldon Brown).
related: Taper fit (Morse taper): a wedge wrapped into a cone; self-holding and knocked apart with a drift wedge (Wikipedia 'Machine taper')
Keyless locking bush (taper-lock bush): tapered rings squeezed by screws instead of hammering, and they keep the hub centred
Mortise and tenon (wedged, drawbored and tusk tenons): the main joinery use of wedges
Wedge dowel (click-in grooved dowel): a ready-made furniture fitting that wedges panels together
Screw thread / lead screw: 'a wedge of considerable length wrapped around a cylinder', self-locking in the same way (Fine Woodworking 1992; IIT Guwahati)
Sprag clutch and roller clutch: wedging elements that lock in one direction only
Binding-plate lock: a tilting plate that wedges on a bar
Eccentric cam lever: a rotating wedge that clamps and releases by hand without a hammer
Dovetail slide with gib strip: a tapered strip (a wedge) adjusted to take up play in a slide
